claim: V3 neurons are defined by postmitotic expression of the transcription factor single-minded homolog 1 (Sim1).
source: These neurons are defined by postmitotic expression of the transcription factor single-minded homolog 1 (Sim1).
evidence: This is a direct statement in the text defining V3 neurons by their expression of Sim1.

claim: V3 neurons are excitatory neurons.
source: They are excitatory neurons, and the majority of them project to the contralateral side of the spinal cord (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: The majority of V3 neurons project to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.
source: They are excitatory neurons, and the majority of them project to the contralateral side of the spinal cord (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: Initial V3 silencing experiments suggested that V3 neurons are involved in the control of locomotion, specifically robustness of the rhythm and left–right coordination.
source: Results from initial V3 silencing experiments suggested that V3 neurons are involved in the control of locomotion, specifically robustness of the rhythm and left–right coordination (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: Prior modeling studies suggest that V3 commissural neurons are involved in promoting left–right synchronization during synchronous gaits.
source: Our prior modeling studies suggest that V3 commissural neurons are involved in promoting left–right synchronization during synchronous gaits (Rybak et al., 2013; Rybak et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015; Danner et al., 2016; Danner et al., 2017) by providing mutual excitation between the extensor half-centers of the left and right lumbar RGs (Danner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citations to multiple prior modeling studies.

claim: V3 commissural neurons provide mutual excitation between the extensor half-centers of the left and right lumbar RGs.
source: Our prior modeling studies suggest that V3 commissural neurons are involved in promoting left–right synchronization during synchronous gaits (Rybak et al., 2013; Rybak et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015; Danner et al., 2016; Danner et al., 2017) by providing mutual excitation between the extensor half-centers of the left and right lumbar RGs (Danner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to Danner et al., 2019.

claim: The V3 population contains distinct subpopulations with different biophysical properties, laminar distributions, and connectivity.
source: Also, these studies did not account for heterogeneity of the V3 population that was shown to contain distinct subpopulations with different biophysical properties, laminar distributions, and connectivity (Borowska et al., 2013; Borowska et al., 2015; Blacklaws et al., 2015; Deska-Gauthier et al., 2020), which may underlie different functions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citations to multiple studies.

claim: A subset of V3 neurons with cell bodies in the lumbar spinal cord have direct excitatory projections to the contralateral side of the cervical enlargement.
source: Here, we identified a subset of V3 neurons with cell bodies in the lumbar spinal cord that have direct excitatory projections to the contralateral side of the cervical enlargement.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by anatomical and electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The recruitment of V3 aLPNs increased with locomotor speed.
source: The recruitment of these neurons increased with locomotor speed.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: V3OFF mice had a significantly reduced maximal locomotor speed.
source: Mice with glutamatergic transmission conditionally knocked out in V3 neurons (V3OFF mice) had significantly reduced maximal speeds of locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: V3OFF mice were unable to move using stable trot, gallop, or bound.
source: V3OFF mice, in which all V3 neurons were silenced, had a significantly reduced maximal locomotor speed, were unable to move using stable trot, gallop, or bound, and predominantly used a lateral-sequence walk.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: V3OFF mice predominantly used a lateral-sequence walk.
source: V3OFF mice, in which all V3 neurons were silenced, had a significantly reduced maximal locomotor speed, were unable to move using stable trot, gallop, or bound, and predominantly used a lateral-sequence walk.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: V3OFF mice lost the ability to trot stably, replacing this most typical mouse gait with a lateral-sequence walk.
source: Moreover, even moving with relatively low and medium speeds, V3OFF mice lost the ability to trot stably, replacing this most typical mouse gait with a lateral-sequence walk.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: At higher locomotor speeds, V3OFF mice exhibited high step-to-step variability of left–right coordination.
source: At higher locomotor speeds, V3OFF mice exhibited high step-to-step variability of left–right coordination, which could be a reason for the speed limitation observed in these animals.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The high step-to-step variability of left–right coordination could be a reason for the speed limitation observed in V3OFF mice.
source: At higher locomotor speeds, V3OFF mice exhibited high step-to-step variability of left–right coordination, which could be a reason for the speed limitation observed in these animals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed data.

claim: The updated model reproduced speed-dependent gait expression in wildtype (WT) mice.
source: The updated model reproduced speed-dependent gait expression in wildtype (WT) mice as well as the experimentally detected changes in the maximal speed, interlimb coordination, and gait expression in V3OFF mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by modeling results in Figures 10-13.

claim: The updated model reproduced the experimentally detected changes in the maximal speed, interlimb coordination, and gait expression in V3OFF mice.
source: The updated model reproduced speed-dependent gait expression in wildtype (WT) mice as well as the experimentally detected changes in the maximal speed, interlimb coordination, and gait expression in V3OFF mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by modeling results in Figures 10-13.

claim: Local V3 CINs mediate left–right interactions within lumbar and cervical cords and promote left–right synchronization necessary for gallop and bound.
source: The model proposes the organization of spinal circuits available for future experimental testing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling results.

claim: V3 aLPNs promote synchronization between diagonal fore and hind RGs necessary for trot.
source: The extended model reproduces our experimental results and suggests that locally projecting V3 neurons, mediating left–right interactions within lumbar and cervical cords, promote left–right synchronization necessary for gallop and bound, whereas the V3 aLPNs promote synchronization between diagonal fore and hind RGs necessary for trot.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling results.

claim: Coordinated rhythmic movement of the limbs during locomotion in mammals is primarily controlled by neural circuitry within the spinal cord.
source: Coordinated rhythmic movement of the limbs during locomotion in mammals is primarily controlled by neural circuitry within the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Each limb is controlled by a separate spinal RG.
source: It is commonly accepted that each limb is controlled by a separate spinal RG (Forssberg et al., 1980; Thibaudier et al., 2013; Frigon, 2017; Danner et al., 2019; Latash et al., 2020) and that RGs controlling left and right forelimbs and left and right hindlimbs are located on the corresponding sides of cervical and lumbar enlargements of the spinal cord, respectively (Kato, 1990; Ballion et al., 2001; Juvin et al., 2005; Juvin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as commonly accepted knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: RGs controlling left and right forelimbs and left and right hindlimbs are located on the corresponding sides of cervical and lumbar enlargements of the spinal cord, respectively.
source: It is commonly accepted that each limb is controlled by a separate spinal RG (Forssberg et al., 1980; Thibaudier et al., 2013; Frigon, 2017; Danner et al., 2019; Latash et al., 2020) and that RGs controlling left and right forelimbs and left and right hindlimbs are located on the corresponding sides of cervical and lumbar enlargements of the spinal cord, respectively (Kato, 1990; Ballion et al., 2001; Juvin et al., 2005; Juvin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: The left and right lumbar and cervical circuits are connected through multiple types of local commissural interneurons (CINs), which coordinate left–right activities.
source: The left and right lumbar and cervical circuits are connected through multiple types of local commissural interneurons (CINs), which coordinate left–right activities (Stein, 1976; Butt and Kiehn, 2003; Quinlan and Kiehn, 2007; Talpalar et al., 2013; Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Rybak et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Descending long propriospinal neuron (dLPNs) and ascending long propriospinal neurons (aLPNs) mediate interactions between cervical and lumbar circuits.
source: In turn, descending long propriospinal neuron (dLPNs) and ascending long propriospinal neurons (aLPNs) mediate interactions between cervical and lumbar circuits (Juvin et al., 2005; Dutton et al., 2006; Reed et al., 2006; Brockett et al., 2013; Ruder et al., 2016; Flynn et al., 2017; Pocratsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Diverse populations of CINs and LPNs are involved in coordination of limb movements, defining locomotor gait, and controlling speed and balance during locomotion.
source: Diverse populations of CINs and LPNs are involved in coordination of limb movements, defining locomotor gait, and controlling speed and balance during locomotion (Danner et al., 2016; Danner et al., 2017; Kiehn, 2016; Ruder et al., 2016; Pocratsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Removal of dLPNs resulted in transient periods of disordered left–right coordination in mice.
source: Removal of dLPNs resulted in transient periods of disordered left–right coordination in mice (Ruder et al., 2016); an effect that our previous computational model (Danner et al., 2017) attributed to excitatory diagonally projecting (commissural) V0V LPNs.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Ruder et al., 2016.

claim: A previous computational model attributed the effect of dLPN removal on left-right coordination to excitatory diagonally projecting (commissural) V0V LPNs.
source: Removal of dLPNs resulted in transient periods of disordered left–right coordination in mice (Ruder et al., 2016); an effect that our previous computational model (Danner et al., 2017) attributed to excitatory diagonally projecting (commissural) V0V LPNs.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Danner et al., 2017.

claim: Experimental silencing of aLPNs was shown to affect left–right coordination in rats in certain locomotor contexts.
source: Similarly, more recent experimental silencing of aLPNs was shown to affect left–right coordination in rats in certain locomotor contexts (Pocratsky et al., 2020); however, the specific populations involved in the effects are unknown.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Pocratsky et al., 2020.

claim: The specific populations involved in the effects of aLPN silencing on left-right coordination are unknown.
source: Similarly, more recent experimental silencing of aLPNs was shown to affect left–right coordination in rats in certain locomotor contexts (Pocratsky et al., 2020); however, the specific populations involved in the effects are unknown.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The excitatory V3 neurons are unlikely to have significant descending propriospinal projections.
source: Although the excitatory V3 neurons are unlikely to have significant descending propriospinal projections (Ruder et al., 2016; Flynn et al., 2017), it remains unknown whether there is a subpopulation of V3 neurons that are aLPNs with involvement in fore–hind and/or left–right interlimb coordination.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Ruder et al., 2016 and Flynn et al., 2017.

claim: V3 aLPNs were almost exclusively located contralaterally to the cervical injection sites.
source: We found that V3 aLPNs were almost exclusively located contralaterally to the cervical injection sites.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: 30% of V3 neurons (n = 3 mice) in L1–L3 were stained by CTB.
source: Overall, 30% of V3 neurons (n = 3 mice) in L1–L3 were stained by CTB but only 12% of V3 neurons in L4 to L6 were CTB positive.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Only 12% of V3 neurons in L4 to L6 were CTB positive.
source: Overall, 30% of V3 neurons (n = 3 mice) in L1–L3 were stained by CTB but only 12% of V3 neurons in L4 to L6 were CTB positive.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The highest density of V3 aLPNs was found in deep dorsal horn, lamina IV to VI, in rostral lumbar segments.
source: Even though clusters of V3 neurons were distributed across ventral to deep dorsal horn (Zhang et al., 2008; Borowska et al., 2013; Borowska et al., 2015; Blacklaws et al., 2015), the highest density of V3 aLPNs was found in deep dorsal horn, lamina IV to VI, in rostral lumbar segments (Figure 1A3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1A3.

claim: A relatively small number of V3 aLPNs were located in the intermediate and ventral regions, lamina VII and VIII, in caudal lumbar segments.
source: A relatively small number of these neurons were located in the intermediate and ventral regions, lamina VII and VIII, in caudal lumbar segments (Figure 1A4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1A4.

claim: Lumbar V3 aLPNs broadly innervate ventral cervical neurons.
source: We detected GFP/TdTom/Vglut2 (vesicular glutamate transporter 2) triple-positive terminals in the ventral interneuron (lamina VII/VIII) and motoneuron (lamina IX) regions (Figure 1B2), indicating that lumbar V3 aLPNs broadly innervate ventral cervical neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B2.

claim: TdTom-positive puncta are ~2.5% of total Vglut2/GFP puncta in the motoneuron region.
source: Interestingly, within the randomly sampled areas in these regions, tdTom-positive puncta are ~2.5% of total Vglut2/GFP puncta in the motoneuron region and ~28% in the interneuron regions (Figure 1B2), indicating that V3 aLPNs may strongly influence cervical RG circuits.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B2.

claim: TdTom-positive puncta are ~28% of total Vglut2/GFP puncta in the interneuron regions.
source: Interestingly, within the randomly sampled areas in these regions, tdTom-positive puncta are ~2.5% of total Vglut2/GFP puncta in the motoneuron region and ~28% in the interneuron regions (Figure 1B2), indicating that V3 aLPNs may strongly influence cervical RG circuits.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B2.

claim: V3 aLPNs may strongly influence cervical RG circuits.
source: Interestingly, within the randomly sampled areas in these regions, tdTom-positive puncta are ~2.5% of total Vglut2/GFP puncta in the motoneuron region and ~28% in the interneuron regions (Figure 1B2), indicating that V3 aLPNs may strongly influence cervical RG circuits.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed data.

claim: Photostimulation of lumbar V3 neurons evoked strong activity in all recorded lumbar and cervical ventral roots.
source: Then, we applied photostimulation to the V3 neurons in the lumbar region. In this case, the stimulation evoked strong activity in all recorded lumbar and cervical ventral roots (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B1 and B2, see also Figure 1C2 and C3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C2, C3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B1 and B2.

claim: Photostimulation of lumbar V3 neurons evoked motor responses in the cervical roots even after blockade of glutamatergic transmission in the lumbar region with kynurenic acid.
source: Then, to test whether this excitation measured in the cervical roots was provided directly by ascending projections of lumbar V3 neurons, we blocked glutamatergic transmission selectively in the lumbar region with 2 mM of kynurenic acid (KA), which completely blocked NMDA and AMPA/kainate receptors (Hägglund et al., 2010). We found that in this case photostimulation of lumbar V3 neurons evoked small or no responses in lumbar ventral roots, while the motor responses in the cervical roots were still present (Figure 1C2 and C3, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C2, C3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lumbar V3 aLPNs directly innervate the cervical spinal cord affecting cervical motor output.
source: Taken together with our anatomical findings, these results demonstrate that lumbar V3 aLPNs directly innervate the cervical spinal cord affecting cervical motor output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical and electrophysiological data presented.

claim: The number of triple-labeled (c-Fos/CTB/tdTom) V3 neurons significantly increased after treadmill locomotion at both speeds compared to animals that only rested.
source: We found that the number of triple-labeled (c-Fos/CTB/tdTom) V3 neurons significantly increased after treadmill locomotion at both speeds compared to animals that only rested, but the percentage of these triple-positive V3 aLPNs almost tripled at 40 cm/s compared to 15 cm/s (Figure 2B1–B3 and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The percentage of triple-positive V3 aLPNs almost tripled at 40 cm/s compared to 15 cm/s.
source: We found that the number of triple-labeled (c-Fos/CTB/tdTom) V3 neurons significantly increased after treadmill locomotion at both speeds compared to animals that only rested, but the percentage of these triple-positive V3 aLPNs almost tripled at 40 cm/s compared to 15 cm/s (Figure 2B1–B3 and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: There are subsets of lumbo-cervical projecting commissural V3 neurons providing direct excitatory drive to cervical locomotor networks, particularly at medium locomotor speeds.
source: Taken together, we conclude that there are subsets of lumbo-cervical projecting commissural V3 neurons providing direct excitatory drive to cervical locomotor networks, particularly at medium locomotor speeds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical and c-Fos data presented.

claim: The highest speed that the V3OFF mice could reach was around 35 cm/s (mean = 34.17 ± 6.69 cm/s).
source: We found that the highest speed that the V3OFF mice could reach was around 35 cm/s (mean = 34.17 ± 6.69 cm/s; Figure 3), and only 3 out of 11 mice could reach 40 cm/s (the maximal speed included for the subsequent analysis).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Only 3 out of 11 V3OFF mice could reach 40 cm/s.
source: We found that the highest speed that the V3OFF mice could reach was around 35 cm/s (mean = 34.17 ± 6.69 cm/s; Figure 3), and only 3 out of 11 mice could reach 40 cm/s (the maximal speed included for the subsequent analysis).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: WT mice could run with speeds up to 75 ± 7.56 cm/s.
source: Under the same experimental conditions, WT mice could run with higher speeds, up to 75 ± 7.56 cm/s (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: V3 neurons are essential for high-speed locomotion in mice.
source: This result indicates that V3 neurons are essential for high-speed locomotion in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the speed limitation data in V3OFF mice.

claim: The left–right hindlimb and forelimb phase differences did not significantly differ between WT and V3OFF mice across speeds.
source: The left–right hindlimb and forelimb phase differences did not significantly differ between WT and V3OFF mice across speeds (Figure 4A1, B1, A2 and B2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B); mean values were close to 0.5 (perfect alternation) in both WT and V3OFF mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Mean values of left-right phase differences were close to 0.5 (perfect alternation) in both WT and V3OFF mice.
source: The left–right hindlimb and forelimb phase differences did not significantly differ between WT and V3OFF mice across speeds (Figure 4A1, B1, A2 and B2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B); mean values were close to 0.5 (perfect alternation) in both WT and V3OFF mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The variability of left–right phase differences in V3OFF mice significantly increased compared to WT mice at higher locomotor speeds.
source: However, the variability of left–right phase differences in V3OFF mice significantly increased compared to WT mice at higher locomotor speeds (Figure 4A2 and B2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The mean values of the homolateral phase differences in V3OFF mice significantly deviated from those in WT mice.
source: In contrast to the left–right phase differences, the mean values of the homolateral (Figure 4C1 and C2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and diagonal phase differences (Figure 4D1 and D2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) in V3OFF mice significantly deviated from those in WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The mean values of the diagonal phase differences in V3OFF mice significantly deviated from those in WT mice.
source: In contrast to the left–right phase differences, the mean values of the homolateral (Figure 4C1 and C2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and diagonal phase differences (Figure 4D1 and D2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) in V3OFF mice significantly deviated from those in WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: At the highest speed (40 cm/s), the difference between the homolateral phase differences was smaller than that at lower speeds but still significant.
source: At the highest speed (40 cm/s), the difference between the homolateral phase differences was smaller than that at lower speeds but still significant, and the diagonal phase differences did not differ significantly.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: At 40 cm/s, the diagonal phase differences did not differ significantly between WT and V3OFF mice.
source: At the highest speed (40 cm/s), the difference between the homolateral phase differences was smaller than that at lower speeds but still significant, and the diagonal phase differences did not differ significantly.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: At least at low to medium speeds, the V3OFF mice were unable to support diagonal synchronization and homolateral alternation.
source: This indicates that, at least at low to medium speeds, the V3OFF mice were unable to support diagonal synchronization and homolateral alternation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phase difference data.

claim: At low treadmill speeds (15 cm/s and 25 cm/s), WT mice mainly used trot.
source: At low treadmill speeds (15 cm/s and 25 cm/s), WT mice mainly used trot (a two-beat gait characterized by diagonal synchronization and left–right alternation; Figure 5B1, e.g., steps x2, x5); however, these are transition speeds and the WT mouse exhibited a comparatively high step-to-step variability with steps that could be classified as different types of walks or even canter (a three-beat gait with only one diagonal synchronized) interspersed (e.g., steps x1, x3, x6) between trot steps.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: At low treadmill speeds (15 cm/s and 25 cm/s), V3OFF mice used a lateral-sequence walk.
source: At the same low treadmill speeds (15 cm/s and 25 cm/s), V3OFF mice used a lateral-sequence walk (a four-beat gait with longer stance than swing phases where the stance of a hindlimb is followed by that of the ipsilateral forelimb; Figure 5B2, e.g., steps x4, x7).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The lateral-sequence walk of V3OFF mice was stable and consistent with little variability between the different step cycles.
source: The lateral-sequence walk of V3OFF mice was stable and consistent with little variability between the different step cycles (Figure 5B2, Figure 5—video 1, Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5 and videos.

claim: At higher treadmill speeds (35 cm/s and 40 cm/s), the step pattern of V3OFF mice became unstable.
source: At higher treadmill speeds (35 cm/s and 40 cm/s), the step pattern of V3OFF mice became unstable (Figure 5B2), while the WT mice exhibited consistent trot steps with little step-to-step variability and good synchronization of the diagonal limbs (Figure 5B1, e.g., steps x8, x9).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: At higher treadmill speeds (35 cm/s and 40 cm/s), WT mice exhibited consistent trot steps with little step-to-step variability and good synchronization of the diagonal limbs.
source: At higher treadmill speeds (35 cm/s and 40 cm/s), the step pattern of V3OFF mice became unstable (Figure 5B2), while the WT mice exhibited consistent trot steps with little step-to-step variability and good synchronization of the diagonal limbs (Figure 5B1, e.g., steps x8, x9).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The variable gait of the V3OFF mice was characterized by steps with various left–right hindlimb and forelimb phase differences, including in-phase steps, and a high step-to-step variability.
source: The variable gait of the V3OFF mice (Figure 5B2) was characterized by steps with various left–right hindlimb and forelimb phase differences (e.g., see episodes y1–3 in Figure 5B2), including in-phase steps, and a high step-to-step variability (Figure 5—video 3, Figure 5—video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5 and videos.

claim: WT mice used trot as the preferred gait at all tested speeds (15–40 cm/s) and its occurrence, persistence, and attractiveness increased with speed.
source: WT mice used trot as the preferred gait at all tested speeds (15–40 cm/s) and its occurrence, persistene, and attractiveness increased with speed (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The most prevalent, persistent, and attractive gait in V3OFF mice at low to medium speeds up to 35 cm/s was a lateral-sequence walk.
source: In contrast, the most prevalent, persistent, and attractive gait in V3OFF mice at low to medium speeds up to 35 cm/s was a lateral-sequence walk (L-walk; Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Although V3OFF animals exhibited steps that could be classified as trot, the occurrence and persistence of trot episodes were low.
source: Although V3OFF animals exhibited steps that could be classified as trot, the occurrence and persistence of trot episodes were low.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: In V3OFF mice the prevalence and attractiveness of the lateral-sequence walk decreased with speed, while the prevalence and attractiveness of less structured out-of-phase walk increased.
source: In contrast, in V3OFF mice the prevalence and attractiveness of the lateral-sequence walk, representing their dominant gait, decreased with speed, while the prevalence and attractiveness of less structured out-of-phase walk increased (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Silencing V3 neurons limited the ability of mice to locomote at high speed.
source: In summary, silencing V3 neurons limited the ability of mice to locomote at high speed (Figure 3), distorted interlimb coordination, and changed homolateral and diagonal phase relationships between fore- and hindlimbs at low and medium speeds (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Silencing V3 neurons distorted interlimb coordination and changed homolateral and diagonal phase relationships between fore- and hindlimbs at low and medium speeds.
source: In summary, silencing V3 neurons limited the ability of mice to locomote at high speed (Figure 3), distorted interlimb coordination, and changed homolateral and diagonal phase relationships between fore- and hindlimbs at low and medium speeds (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Silencing V3 neurons resulted in converting gaits in V3OFF mice from trot to lateral-sequence walk at lower speeds and significantly reduced gait stability when speed increased.
source: This resulted in converting gaits in V3OFF mice from trot to lateral-sequence walk at lower speeds and significantly reduced gait stability when speed increased (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The present computational model was built based on previous models.
source: The present computational model of spinal circuits was built based on our previous models (Danner et al., 2017; Danner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citations.

claim: The RG populations contained 200 neurons each; all other populations contained 100 neurons.
source: The RG populations contained 200 neurons each; all other populations contained 100 neurons.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The local V3 CINs are involved in excitatory interactions between left and right extensor (V3-E) and left and right flexor (V3-F) half-centers within both cervical and lumbar compartments.
source: The local V3 CINs are involved in excitatory interactions between left and right extensor (V3-E) and left and right flexor (V3-F) half-centers within both cervical and lumbar compartments (Rybak et al., 2013; Rybak et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015; Danner et al., 2016; Danner et al., 2017; Danner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The V3 aLPNs (aV3) mediate the diagonal (commissural) pathways from lumbar to cervical RGs.
source: The V3 aLPNs (aV3) mediate the diagonal (commissural) pathways from lumbar to cervical RGs, which have been incorporated based on our experimental results (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and based on experimental results in Figure 1.

claim: Increasing the brainstem drive caused an increase in frequency of locomotor oscillations and consecutive gait transitions from lateral-sequence walk to trot and finally to bound.
source: Increasing the brainstem drive caused an increase in frequency of locomotor oscillations and consecutive gait transitions from lateral-sequence walk (Figure 10A1) to trot (Figure 10A2) and finally to bound (Figure 10A3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by modeling results in Figure 10.

claim: The increase of V3 population activity with the increase of locomotor frequency was consistent with experimental results.
source: This increase of V3 population activity with the increase of locomotor frequency (reflecting locomotor speed) was consistent with our experimental results (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text comparing modeling results to experimental data.

claim: Increasing brainstem drive in the intact model resulted in sequential changes of gait from lateral-sequence walk to trot and then to gallop and bound.
source: Increasing brainstem drive in the intact model resulted in sequential changes of gait from lateral-sequence walk to trot and then to gallop and bound (Figure 11A1) and was accompanied by increased frequency of stable locomotor oscillations (Figure 11B1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by modeling results in Figure 11.

claim: The sequential gait changes in the model were consistent with previous experimental observations and modeling studies.

claim: Two subgroups of lumbar V3 neurons, which possess local projections or long ascending propriospinal commissural projections, are essential components in the locomotor circuits that promote speed-dependent interlimb synchronization to provide stable locomotion at different speed and gaits.
source: Nevertheless, here, we took advantage of available experimental and computational tools to demonstrate that two subgroups of lumbar V3 neurons, which possess local projections or long ascending propriospinal commissural projections, are essential components in the locomotor circuits that promote speed-dependent interlimb synchronization to provide stable locomotion at different speed and gaits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.
